conceptTag: Switching costs from the customer's side
readerTitle: Why a 25% cheaper offer still loses
caseNote: 가상 사례 (회계·장부 대행 회사, 사내 운영팀의 경비 정산 도구) + 실제 연구 (Burnham, Frels & Mahajan 2003의 전환 비용 유형). 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 고객은 새 제안을 지금 내는 가격과 비교하지 않는다. 지금 가격에 '옮기는 비용'을 더한 것과 비교하며, 그 비용은 파는 쪽이 대신 줄여 줄 수 있다.
misconception: 더 싸고 더 좋으면 고객은 옮긴다. 안 옮기는 고객은 비합리적이거나 충성도가 높은 것이다.

sources.text: Burnham, T. A., Frels, J. K., & Mahajan, V. (2003). Consumer switching costs: A typology, antecedents, and consequences. Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 31(2), 109–126.

factChecks.note: Burnham, Frels & Mahajan(2003)의 전환 비용 분류(절차적 procedural, 재무적 financial, 관계적 relational)와 서지 정보(JAMS 31권 2호)를 게시 전에 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 세 가지 유형 이름만 쓰고 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.
전환 비용을 대신 떠안은 경우: 직원 시간 $2,000과 겹치는 달 $750을 회사가 부담하면 고객 비용은 $1,500 + $1,000 = $2,500. 첫해 결과 $3,000 − $2,500 = +$500.
사내 도구: 직원 1인당 월 10분 절약, 학습 1시간(60분) → 60 ÷ 10 = 6개월 후에야 본전. 200명 기준 월 2,000분(약 33시간) 절약.

cards.title: Why a 25% cheaper offer still loses
body: Your firm offers a small manufacturer the same bookkeeping for $9,000 a year. Their current firm charges $12,000.
They say no. They aren't confused, and they aren't blindly loyal. They simply did different math than you did.

image.label: Two price tags, with a heavy box sitting on the cheaper one
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 가격표 두 개: "$12,000"과 "$9,000". 더 싼 가격표 위에 "Moving"이라고 적힌 무거운 상자가 얹혀 저울이 비싼 쪽으로 기울지 않음. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: They like you. They still said "not now."
body: You run a bookkeeping firm. A prospect pays their current firm $12,000 a year. You offer the same service for $9,000.
They're friendly, but they keep saying now isn't a good time. What do you change?

options.text: Cut the price to $7,500 so the saving is impossible to ignore
options.feedback: A bigger saving can tip the balance, but you give up margin every year to solve a problem that mostly lives in the first few months.

options.text: Offer to collect their records, run the handover and cover the first month
options.feedback: You spend effort once and remove the costs that made them hesitate. The next card shows what those costs look like.

options.text: Wait and call back when their current contract ends
options.feedback: Good timing lowers the cost of leaving. But the handover work will still be waiting for them when you call.

cards.title: The prospect's math, year one.
body: You saw a $3,000 saving. They saw a year-one loss of **$2,250**. At this rate, switching only pays for itself after about 21 months.

breakdown.label: Staff time
breakdown.detail: 40 hours gathering records, at $50 an hour

breakdown.label: Owner time
breakdown.detail: 20 hours learning a new process, at $75 an hour

breakdown.label: Overlap month
breakdown.detail: Paying the new firm while the old one finishes

breakdown.label: Risk allowance
breakdown.detail: A guess at the cost of mistakes during handover

breakdown.label: Year one
breakdown.detail: What switching actually does to them this year

cards.title: Switching costs
body: **Switching costs** are everything a customer spends or gives up to move from what they use now to you, beyond your price. Time, effort, risk, fees, lost relationships.

Customers compare your offer to their current option *plus* the cost of getting out of it. So your offer must beat the old one by more than the switching cost, and usually within a time they care about.

image.label: Scale: yearly saving on one side, switching costs on the other
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 접시에 "Saving $3,000" 동전 더미, 오른쪽 접시에 "Staff time", "Owner time", "Overlap", "Risk" 블록 네 개. 오른쪽이 더 무겁게 기울어짐.

cards.title: Three kinds of cost, most of them invisible to you.
body: Marketing researchers Burnham, Frels and Mahajan (2003) sorted switching costs into three groups:
list: **Procedural:** time and effort to search, set up and learn
**Financial:** fees, overlap payments, lost discounts or points
**Relational:** losing a person or team you already trust
cards.callout: Only one of these shows up on your price list. The customer feels all three.

cards.title: You can pay the switching cost for them.
body: Suppose your firm gathers the records itself. You do this often, so it takes you far less time than it takes them. You also cover the overlap month.
Their cost drops to $1,500 of owner time plus the $1,000 risk allowance: **$2,500**. Now year one shows +$500, and every year after saves $3,000.
cards.softwareNote: In software, this looks like importing a customer's old data, keeping their existing links working, or setting up the account for them. A one-time effort for you can remove months of hesitation for them.

cards.title: High switching costs keep customers, not their goodwill.
body: The same idea works in reverse. If your own customers stay mainly because leaving is painful, they aren't happy. They're stuck. They tend to leave the moment a rival makes switching easy.
Also, your estimate is not their estimate. Ask customers what moving would really involve. The cost they fear, like a botched year-end, may matter more than the hours.

cards.title: Now it's your own company's staff.
body: You lead an internal operations team. You built a new expense tool that saves each of 200 employees about 10 minutes a month over the old spreadsheet.
Learning it takes about an hour, and open reports must be re-entered by hand. Few people use it. What do you do?

options.text: Make it mandatory from next month
options.feedback: You get usage fast, but people still pay the full switching cost, and resentment can follow the tool for years.

options.text: Import old reports automatically and run a 15-minute walkthrough
options.feedback: An hour of learning against 10 minutes saved means six months before anyone breaks even. Cut the cost of moving, and the payoff arrives in weeks.

options.text: Add more features so the saving gets bigger
options.feedback: More features often mean more to learn, which raises the switching cost you're trying to beat.

cards.title: Customers buy the move, not just the product.
body: A better offer only wins when its gain beats the cost of switching. Shrink that cost, and you often don't need to cut your price.
**Try it today:** pick one prospect who said "not now." List the time, money and risk moving to you would cost them. Choose one item you could take off their plate.
